blocks.text: A 24-year-old man collapses at a restaurant fifteen minutes after eating a dessert. He has hives over his trunk, a swollen lip, a wheeze and a pulse of 130 beats per minute with a falling blood pressure. The single most important thing a bystander with medical training can do in the next minute is give an injection into his thigh.

blocks.markdown: **Allergy** is a hypersensitivity reaction initiated by specific immunological mechanisms, usually IgE (type I), to an otherwise harmless antigen (an **allergen**). **Atopy** is the genetic predisposition to produce IgE against common environmental allergens; atopic people are prone to **allergic rhinitis, asthma and eczema**, and often to food allergy. **Sensitisation** (detectable specific IgE) is not the same as allergy: many people are sensitised but have no symptoms on exposure.

blocks.title: Anaphylaxis
blocks.text: A serious, rapid-onset, generalised or systemic hypersensitivity reaction that can be life-threatening. Most often IgE-mediated, in which allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, tryptase and other mediators. Common triggers include foods, insect venom and drugs.

blocks.markdown:
**Features.** Anaphylaxis typically begins within minutes (sometimes up to an hour or two) of exposure. Cardinal features are involvement of **airway, breathing or circulation** (ABC), usually with skin or mucosal signs:

- **Airway:** swelling of the tongue or throat, hoarse voice, stridor.
- **Breathing:** wheeze, breathlessness.
- **Circulation:** hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, collapse, from vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
- **Skin and mucosa:** urticaria (hives), flushing, angioedema (present in most, but may be absent).
- **Gastrointestinal:** vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.

A **biphasic** reaction can occur, in which symptoms recur hours later even without re-exposure. Serum **mast cell tryptase** measured within a few hours of the event (compared with a baseline) can support the diagnosis.

blocks.title: First-line treatment
blocks.text: Remove the trigger if possible, call for help, lay the patient flat (legs raised; sit up if breathing difficulty; recovery position if unconscious), and give **adrenaline (epinephrine) intramuscularly into the anterolateral mid-thigh** without delay. Give oxygen and intravenous fluids. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts and do not treat airway obstruction or shock. Repeat adrenaline after about 5 minutes if there is no improvement, as per the guideline in use. Observe afterwards because of the biphasic reaction.

blocks.markdown: **Why adrenaline works.** Adrenaline acts on several receptors that oppose what mast cell mediators do: **α1** causes vasoconstriction, raising blood pressure and reducing mucosal oedema; **β1** increases heart rate and contractility; **β2** relaxes bronchial smooth muscle (bronchodilation) and decreases further release of mediators from mast cells. It therefore treats all three components of the reaction: airway swelling, bronchospasm and shock.

**Why intramuscular?** The **intramuscular** route, into the vastus lateralis in the lateral thigh, gives rapid and reliable absorption because skeletal muscle is richly perfused, and it can be given by non-specialists and by auto-injector. **Subcutaneous** injection is absorbed more slowly, particularly in a shocked, vasoconstricted patient, as adrenaline itself reduces local blood flow. **Intravenous** adrenaline can cause dangerous arrhythmias and hypertension, needs monitoring and titration, and is reserved for specialist settings (for example refractory shock under expert supervision).

blocks.title: Pharmacology teaching example: adrenaline volume
blocks.prompt: (Teaching example of dose arithmetic only, not clinical advice.) Adrenaline for intramuscular use is supplied at 1 mg per mL (a '1 in 1000' solution). A teaching dose of 0.5 mg is to be drawn up. What volume is needed, and why does the concentration label matter?

steps.text: Express the 1 in 1000 label as a concentration: 1 g in 1000 mL.
Volume equals dose divided by concentration.
Emphasise the hazard: the weaker '1 in 10,000' solution (0.1 mg/mL) is for specialist intravenous use, and confusing the two strengths causes ten-fold errors.

blocks.answer: 0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL (1 in 1000) adrenaline; the concentration determines the volume.

blocks.caption: Principles of allergen testing

blocks.markdown: **Interpreting tests.** A positive test shows only **sensitisation**; the history of reactions on exposure decides whether it is clinically relevant. A positive result with no symptoms on eating the food does not mean the food must be avoided; tests with a negative history can be misleading. **Desensitisation (allergen immunotherapy)** is the repeated administration of gradually increasing doses of allergen, under specialist supervision, to induce tolerance. It shifts the response from Th2/IgE towards regulatory T cells and IgG4 blocking antibodies, and reduces the symptoms of insect venom allergy and allergic rhinitis. It carries a risk of systemic reaction and is not suitable for everyone, for example poorly controlled asthma.

blocks.title: Weighing a test result
blocks.prompt: A 6-year-old has asthma and eczema. A serum specific IgE to egg is positive, but she eats well-cooked egg in cake regularly without symptoms. Should egg be strictly avoided? Explain.

steps.text: Recognise what the test measures: specific IgE shows sensitisation, not clinical reactivity.
Weigh the history: she tolerates egg in cake with no symptoms, so she does not have a clinical allergy to egg in that form.
Conclude that the result is not clinically relevant on its own; unnecessary avoidance can have costs including lost tolerance. If doubt remains, a supervised challenge can resolve it.
Note atopy: the positive IgE is consistent with her atopic background.

blocks.answer: No: sensitisation without clinical reaction does not justify strict avoidance.

items: Atopy: IgE predisposition with eczema, asthma, rhinitis.
Anaphylaxis: ABC compromise plus skin signs; treat with IM adrenaline.
IM route: fast and reliable absorption; SC slower in shock; IV risky.
Tests show sensitisation; challenge and history decide; immunotherapy induces tolerance.

points: Anaphylaxis presents with airway, breathing or circulation compromise, usually with urticaria or angioedema; first-line treatment is intramuscular adrenaline into the mid-thigh.
Adrenaline reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm and mucosal oedema (α1, β1, β2); IM gives rapid, reliable absorption, unlike subcutaneous in shock or IV outside specialist care.
Skin-prick and specific IgE tests show sensitisation, not allergy; supervised challenge and history confirm; immunotherapy induces tolerance via regulatory T cells and IgG4.

distractorRationale.b: Correct: serious systemic reaction with ABC involvement.
distractorRationale.c: This describes type IV contact dermatitis.
distractorRationale.d: Chronic urticaria alone is not anaphylaxis.

questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid systemic allergic reaction with life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually accompanied by urticaria or angioedema.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is stung by a wasp and within 10 minutes develops stridor, diffuse hives and a systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg. What is the first-line drug and route?

distractorRationale.a: Antihistamines are adjuncts and act too slowly for airway or circulatory compromise.
distractorRationale.c: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and unreliable in shock.
distractorRationale.d: Corticosteroids act slowly and do not reverse airway oedema or shock.

questions.explanation: Intramuscular adrenaline is first-line, treating airway oedema, bronchospasm and hypotension. Antihistamines and steroids are secondary and do not reverse life-threatening features.

questions.stem: Which receptor effect of adrenaline helps to reverse hypotension in anaphylaxis?

distractorRationale.a: β2 causes bronchodilation and some vasodilation, which does not raise pressure.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: α1 vasoconstriction increases peripheral resistance and reduces leak.
distractorRationale.c: Adrenaline does not act at muscarinic receptors and bradycardia would worsen shock.
distractorRationale.d: H1 agonism would worsen the reaction.

questions.explanation: Adrenaline acts on α1 receptors causing vasoconstriction, β1 receptors for increased cardiac output, and β2 receptors for bronchodilation.

questions.stem: Why is intramuscular preferred over subcutaneous injection of adrenaline in anaphylaxis?

options.text: Muscle is better perfused, giving faster and more reliable absorption
Intramuscular adrenaline has no cardiac effects
The subcutaneous route requires specialist monitoring

questions.correctOptionText: Muscle is better perfused, giving faster and more reliable absorption

distractorRationale.a: Correct: muscle blood flow is high, whereas adrenaline vasoconstricts subcutaneous tissue, slowing uptake.
distractorRationale.b: Subcutaneous adrenaline is active but slower.
distractorRationale.c: IM adrenaline does affect the heart (β1).

questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is richly perfused, so IM adrenaline reaches the circulation rapidly and predictably, whereas absorption from subcutaneous tissue is slow, especially in shock.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive specific IgE to peanut but has eaten peanuts regularly without problems. What does this indicate?

options.text: Sensitisation without clinical allergy; the test alone does not establish allergy

questions.correctOptionText: Sensitisation without clinical allergy; the test alone does not establish allergy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sensitisation must be interpreted with the history.
distractorRationale.b: A tolerated exposure argues against clinical allergy.
distractorRationale.c: IgE-mediated sensitisation is not type IV.

questions.explanation: A positive specific IgE or skin-prick test indicates sensitisation. Without symptoms on exposure, the patient is not clinically allergic.

questions.stem: True or false: allergen immunotherapy (desensitisation) works by increasing allergen-specific IgE.
questions.explanation: Immunotherapy shifts responses toward regulatory T cells and IgG4 blocking antibodies and reduces mast cell reactivity. It is done under specialist supervision.

questions.stem: Teaching example only: a child weighing 25 kg is used in a dose-arithmetic exercise with an intramuscular adrenaline dose of 0.01 mg/kg. The solution is 1 mg/mL. What volume in mL is needed?
questions.explanation: The dose is 0.01 mg/kg × 25 kg = 0.25 mg. Volume = 0.25 mg ÷ 1 mg/mL = 0.25 mL. This is arithmetic for teaching, and real doses follow current local guidelines.

questions.stem: Teaching example only: a 10 mL prefilled syringe contains adrenaline labelled '1 in 10,000'. How many milligrams of adrenaline does the whole syringe contain?
questions.explanation: A 1 in 10,000 solution is 1 g in 10,000 mL, which is 0.1 mg/mL. In 10 mL there is 0.1 × 10 = 1 mg. This weaker solution is for specialist intravenous use, and mistaking it for the 1 mg/mL IM solution would give a ten-fold error.
